edits.quote: Shape Detectives!
edits.fix: Delete the extra page title. The page should go from the header straight to the shared rules and Problem 1.

edits.quote: Today you’ll become a shape detective and discover how pieces fit together!
edits.fix: Delete. It is cutesy narration and does no mathematical work.

edits.quote: Turn them to fit, with no gaps or overlaps. (repeated on p3 as "Turn the pieces as needed.")
edits.fix: State the activity-wide rule once, unnumbered, at the top of page 1 (for example, "Fill each shape with pattern blocks: no gaps, no overlaps, nothing sticking out"). Remove the rule from P1 and P3.

edits.quote: Fill the sailboat and the cat. Use any small pieces.
edits.fix: With any pieces allowed, the sailboat (11 triangle spaces) and the cat (7) take a minute or two each. Give them a target, for example "Fill each one with as few pieces as you can, then with as many as you can" (the hexagon fits across the sail and hull), so the outlines support real work.

edits.quote: Ask an adult to trace your pieces before you lift them to use again.
edits.fix: Delete. Each shape has two outlines, and there are plenty of blocks, so nothing needs lifting. If tracing is wanted, put it in the adult notes.

edits.quote: Great job! You’re a tiling superstar!
edits.fix: Delete the generic encouragement.

edits.quote: Fill each shape two different ways.
edits.fix: Two ways is trivial (one way for the hexagon is just the yellow hexagon). Ask for as many different fillings as they can find, or all fillings that use exactly three pieces. Add a few more compact outlines, or use the trace-and-color recording.

edits.quote: Turn the pieces as needed. Use them again for the next shape.
edits.fix: Delete. The turning rule is shared and belongs at the top, and the reuse direction is unnecessary.

edits.quote: Hint: Start at the pointy tip of the arrow and work your way in.
edits.fix: Delete the hint. Adults can give it if needed.

edits.quote: Arrow (2-wide arrow outline, exactly two chevrons nested side by side)
edits.fix: The arrow is solved at once by laying two chevrons side by side. Keep the star, which takes 3 chevrons around alternate inner corners. Replace the arrow with a shape chevrons cannot fill (for example the P2 diamond: its pointed corners can't hold a chevron) and ask "Can you fill it with only chevrons?"

edits.quote: Bonus Challenge
edits.fix: Delete the label. It marks P4–P5 as optional, so for many children the K–1 sheet effectively ends on page 3, and the problems are no harder than P1–P3.

edits.quote: Then fill it again with any small pieces you like.
edits.fix: Replace the filler follow-up with "Find three different ways to fill the long hexagon with only blue rhombi". Exactly three exist, so a child knows when they are done. Add two compact copies of the outline.

edits.quote: Fill the mountain using only small green triangles. Then fill it again with any small pieces you like.
edits.fix: Nine green triangles in a 3-edge triangle is trivial. Replace with the kernel-1 entry point: "Try to fill the mountain with only blue rhombi. What happens? How few green triangles can you get away with?" The answer is 3, because there are 6 up-triangles and 3 down. This is the only place K–1 would meet the session's main idea.

edits.quote: Packet ends after P5 (about 18 minutes of work for a quick child)
edits.fix: About 22 minutes are missing for a quick child. Design a first block of new substantial problems, for example "Which of these outlines can be filled with only blue rhombi?" (a mix of possible, odd-area, and even-but-impossible shapes at actual size).

edits.quote: Packet ends after P5 (about 18 minutes of work for a quick child)
edits.fix: Second block of missing minutes. Add another open problem, for example finding all the ways to fill the yellow-hexagon outline with blocks, or building the next bigger mountain or hexagon from upscale blocks and filling it with small ones.

k-1.summary: Four pages of outline-filling puzzles at correct actual size, but nearly every task is a one- or two-minute fill with any pieces, and the session's kernels are never touched (P5 uses only triangles where the blue-only version would show the up/down obstruction). The worksheet carries a title, a cutesy intro, praise, a hint and a "Bonus Challenge" label, and it runs out after about 18 minutes for a quick child: exactly the organizer's "too dumbed down, ends too early" complaint.

edits.quote: The Great Board Mystery
edits.fix: Delete the second page title above Problem 1.

edits.quote: Remember: tiling isn’t just about filling space, it’s about seeing hidden patterns!
edits.fix: Delete. It is a "not X, but Y" turn that does no work.

edits.quote: Keep pieces inside the board without overlaps. / without overlaps or pieces outside / Keep pieces inside the triangle without overlaps. / Cover whole triangle spaces without overlaps or pieces outside.
edits.fix: Write one unnumbered shared-rules line at the top of page 1 (pieces cover whole triangle spaces, no overlaps, nothing outside the board). Remove the four restatements from P1, P2 (twice) and P3.

edits.quote: Boards A–D: A is a 3-edge triangle (9 spaces), B a 2x3 parallelogram (12), C an 11-space board, D a long hexagon (10)
edits.fix: Both impossible boards (A and C) have an odd number of triangle spaces, so "What is stopping you?" has only the trivial parity answer. The hidden up/down obstruction never appears in P1, and Board A duplicates the 3-edge triangle in P2. Replace A (or C) with an even-area board that has two more up-triangles than down-triangles, for example the 1-2-3 trapezoid (8 spaces, 5 up and 3 down), so P1 sets up the real question.

edits.quote: Hint: Color the triangles that point up and the triangles that point down, then count each kind.
edits.fix: Delete. The hint prints the intended discovery (the coloring argument) as a procedure. Move it to the adult notes.

edits.quote: 2 small edges on each side / 3 small edges on each side / 4 small edges on each side / 5 small edges on each side
edits.fix: Delete the size captions. The gridded diagrams already show the size.

edits.quote: Problem 2: Fit as many small blue rhombi as you can in this triangle. Keep pieces inside the triangle without overlaps. Record your best packing.
edits.fix: Page 3 repeats the "Problem 2:" label and restates the task and rules. Let the 5-edge triangle continue P2 with no second label and no restated directions. Also drop "Record how many blues fit and how many triangle spaces stay empty" on p2, because the labeled blanks already say this.

edits.quote: Compare your four best packings. What do you notice about the number of empty spaces? Explain why you cannot leave fewer.
edits.fix: Cut the generic compare/notice prompt to the real question: "What is the fewest number of empty spaces for each triangle? Explain why you cannot leave fewer." Optionally add "What about a triangle with 10 small edges on each side?"

edits.quote: Fewest empty triangle spaces: / Blues: ____ Purples: ____
edits.fix: In P2, "Blues:" meant the number of rhombi placed. Here it apparently means the fewest empty spaces with blues, and "Fewest empty triangle spaces:" has no blank of its own. Relabel as "Empty spaces with blues: ___  Empty spaces with purples: ___".

edits.quote: Boards A, C, E (A and C are 3-wide and 2-wide arrows that nest perfectly with both pieces; E is board C plus one triangle)
edits.fix: A and C give 0/0 in under a minute each, and E gives 1/1 for a trivial odd-area reason. Keep B (0 vs 4), D (0 vs 2) and F (2 vs 4), which contrast. Replace two of A/C/E with boards where purples leave strictly more gaps than blues, or where blues leave an even number of gaps (for example the 4-edge triangle).

edits.quote: Can you cover one purple exactly with blues? How does this explain which pieces can leave fewer gaps?
edits.fix: The first question walks the child to the answer. Replace both with "Is there any board where purples leave fewer empty spaces than blues? Explain." Add writing lines, since there is no answer space on the page.

edits.quote: Fun fact: Mathematicians call this kind of argument a coloring proof!
edits.fix: Delete. It is a "Fun fact" box, and it is misplaced: the chevron argument above it (each purple splits into two blues) is a decomposition argument, while the coloring proof was P2's.

edits.quote: Blank page 5 (footer only, no header, no content)
edits.fix: Delete the empty page.

grades-2-3.summary: This band delivers kernel 1 well: possible versus impossible boards, then the n-gap bound on triangles of side 2–5 (all boards at correct actual size), then blues versus chevrons. The B, D and F results (0/4, 0/2, 2/4) contrast correctly. The P2 hint gives away the coloring discovery. P1's impossible boards are odd-area, so the hidden obstruction never appears there, P3 pads with near-duplicate arrows, and a title, a "not X but Y" line, a Fun fact box, repeated rules and a blank page need removing.

edits.quote: Welcome, tiling explorers! In this activity, you will discover the secret world of flips.
edits.fix: Delete the cutesy intro and meta narration.

edits.quote: Find as many different tilings as you can. ... How many different tilings did you find?
edits.fix: "As many as you can" gives no stopping point. Ask "Find all the tilings. How do you know you have found them all?" There are exactly 6 for this 1-2-2 hexagon, so a child can finish and justify.

edits.quote: Six cards A–F showing all six tilings, printed on the page right after P1
edits.fix: The cards are correct (all six distinct tilings, and the A→B flip example matches cards A and B), but they reveal P1's full answer. Print them on a separate sheet the adult hands out after P1, or have children cut out and label their own P1 recordings.

edits.quote: Can you get from every card to every other card by a sequence of flips? Explain your thinking.
edits.fix: Drop "Explain your thinking". Once the map is drawn, the connection question answers itself on the map.

edits.quote: Find the shortest route from A to F. Write the cards you visit and count your flips. Explain your thinking.
edits.fix: Once the map is drawn (A-B, B-C, B-D, C-E, D-E, E-F), the 4-flip route is a 30-second read-off, so this is not a 5-minute problem. Fold it into P2, or ask why no route shorter than 4 flips can exist. Drop the boilerplate "Explain your thinking".

edits.quote: Explain what you notice.
edits.fix: Tighten to "Can you leave A and return to A in an odd number of flips? Why or why not?" (The answer is no: the flip graph is bipartite.)

edits.quote: Part 2: Ribbons, the Secret Code
edits.fix: Delete the section heading. Only "Problem N:" labels belong on the page.

edits.quote: Card A label sits on the top edge where the example ribbon's arrowhead ends
edits.fix: Move the "A" label up or to the side so it does not collide with the dashed ribbon.

edits.quote: Follow these steps. (a) Count the L’s in each code. (b) Count the R’s in each code. (c) Add them up. (d) Look at how many edges the board has on its left and right sides, and use that to explain why.
edits.fix: Replace the four directed sub-steps, whose last one ("explain why") never says what is to be explained, with one question: "What do all six codes have in common? Explain it from the shape of the board."

edits.quote: Write every different order you can make with two L’s and two R’s. Match each order to a tiling card.
edits.fix: An unnumbered task under P7 that also prints P7's answer (two L's, two R's) and, with its six slots, the count. Since every card already has its code written in P5/P6, the matching is just copying. Make it its own problem asking "Does every order of two L's and two R's come from exactly one tiling?", or merge it into P8.

edits.quote: Rebuild the tiling from each ribbon. Draw the four blue rhombi crossed by the ribbon, then fill the remaining spaces with blue rhombi. (ribbons RLLR and LLRR)
edits.fix: The two ribbons are RLLR and LLRR, the codes of cards D and F, which are already drawn with their codes, so the rebuild is a copy job. The sentence also dictates the method. Use ribbons on a larger hexagon whose tilings are not on the page (for example the 2-2-2 hexagon with two ribbons). Keep only "Rebuild the tiling. Can a ribbon give two different tilings?"

edits.quote: Problem 9: Compare the ribbon codes before and after each flip on your map. What changes? Write three examples. / Problem 10: Circle every neighboring RL or LR in your six codes. ... Check with the cards and blocks, then describe your rule.
edits.fix: Merge into one problem without the directed steps (circle, check, write three examples): "How does one flip change the ribbon code? Does every such change come from a flip? Use this to explain your answer to Problem 4." This adds the missing payoff, since each flip swaps one adjacent L/R pair, so round trips are even.

grades-4-5.summary: A strong, correct development of kernel 2. All six tilings of the 1-2-2 hexagon are drawn correctly, the flip example matches, the flip map (one 4-cycle, bipartite) supports the shortest-route and odd-round-trip questions, and every card's ribbon code checks out. The sequence is chopped into directed sub-steps, though (P7 a–d, P8's method, P9/P10 circling), P3 and P8 are trivial read-offs or copies, the cards give away P1's answer, and the welcome line, "Secret Code" heading and repeated "Explain your thinking" read as machine-written.

overall.strongest: The grades 4–5 pages carry the outline's flip-graph and ribbon ideas through a correct, well-ordered sequence with accurate diagrams and actual-size boards, and grades 2–3 is a close second.
overall.weakest: The K–1 pages are a short run of trivial fill-the-outline tasks (about 18 minutes for a quick child) with cutesy title, praise and a Bonus label, and they never reach the session's ideas, so they need new problems rather than trimming.
